name: Zuranolone

lead: Zuranolone (Zurzuvae) is a prescription capsule taken as a 14-day course for postpartum depression. It is a lab-made relative of allopregnanolone, a steroid the brain makes from progesterone. Interest in it for looks runs through mood and sleep: calmer, better-rested people tend to look more relaxed.

It enhances the inhibitory action of GABA at GABA-A receptors through a neurosteroid binding site. In phase 3 trials in postpartum depression, patients on zuranolone had greater reductions in depression scores than placebo at day 15. It has not been studied for appearance.

paras: It is prescribed as a single short course for postpartum depression in adults. It is positioned as an oral alternative to intravenous brexanolone.

The label has a boxed warning for impaired driving and lists sleepiness, dizziness and fatigue as common effects. It also warns about suicidal thoughts and possible fetal harm. It is prescription-only and Schedule IV in the US.

social.title: How Zuranolone, a Fast-Acting Drug, Might Help Those Suffering with Postpartum Depression

angle.text: Zuranolone is an approved postpartum depression drug that comes up in neurosteroid and mood-recovery discussions. The route to looks is mood and sleep relief leading to a more rested, relaxed appearance. Trials have studied it for depression.

lead: Zuranolone (brand name Zurzuvae) is an oral neuroactive steroid that acts as a positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A receptors. It is a synthetic analog of the body's own neurosteroid allopregnanolone and was developed by Sage Therapeutics with Biogen. The US FDA approved it in August 2023 for postpartum depression in adults, a 14-day oral course positioned as an alternative to intravenous brexanolone.[1][2][3]

Zuranolone has no approved or studied use for appearance. It appears on the wiki as a recovery-category neurosteroid, in the context of community interest in mood, anxiety and sleep. Its US label carries a boxed warning about impaired driving and other hazardous activities, and it is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US.[2][3][4]

In published phase 3 trials in postpartum depression, patients given zuranolone showed greater reductions in depression scores than placebo at day 15. For major depressive disorder, the FDA issued a complete response letter citing insufficient evidence of effectiveness, while Japan approved it for depression in 2026.[5][6][3]
infobox: Neuroactive steroid; GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulator

paras: The only US-approved indication is postpartum depression (PPD) in adults. The label describes zuranolone as a neuroactive steroid GABA-A receptor positive modulator, taken as a once-daily 14-day course.[2] The European Commission authorised it for PPD in September 2025, and Japan has approved it for depression.[1][3]

Investigational uses reported include bipolar depression, insomnia with depression, essential tremor and Parkinson's disease; registered studies also cover post-stroke depression and adolescent pharmacokinetics.[3][7][8][9]

Zuranolone enhances inhibitory signalling through both synaptic and extrasynaptic GABA-A receptors by binding a neurosteroid site distinct from the benzodiazepine site.[1][4] The label states that how this produces an effect in PPD is not fully understood.[2] Reviews describe neurosteroid GABA-A modulators as a distinct approach from monoaminergic antidepressants.[10][11]

Zuranolone is absorbed orally, with exposure increased by food; it is highly protein-bound and mainly metabolised by CYP3A4, so strong CYP3A4 inhibitors and inducers change its levels. Its half-life is roughly 16 to 25 hours, supporting once-daily dosing, compared with about 9 hours for intravenous brexanolone.[1][3][12]

The label lists somnolence, dizziness, diarrhea, fatigue, nasopharyngitis and urinary tract infection as the most common adverse reactions.[2] A boxed warning states that it causes driving impairment through CNS depressant effects, and advises against driving or hazardous activities for at least 12 hours after a dose during the treatment course.[2]
The label also warns of suicidal thoughts and behaviour, and of possible fetal harm, and describes a pregnancy exposure registry.[2]

Zuranolone (development code SAGE-217) grew out of work on allopregnanolone, whose intravenous form brexanolone was approved in 2019 for PPD and later withdrawn from the US market. Zuranolone was designed for oral use.[3][13] Preclinical characterisation described it as a selective neuroactive steroid GABA-A modulator.[12] US approval followed in August 2023, and Supernus Pharmaceuticals acquired Sage in 2025, according to one reference.[1][3]

Zuranolone is prescription-only. In the US it is a Schedule IV controlled substance.[3] Online community material on the compound is scarce; interest centres on neurosteroids as a class for stress, mood and sleep.

Two phase 3 randomised placebo-controlled trials in PPD reported greater improvement on the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale with zuranolone than with placebo at day 15, including a 2021 JAMA Psychiatry trial and a 2023 American Journal of Psychiatry trial in severe PPD.[5][6][1]

In major depressive disorder, phase 3 trials including MOUNTAIN and a later placebo-controlled study have been published, and the FDA declined to approve it for this use, citing insufficient evidence of effectiveness.[14][15][3] Reviews describe the neurosteroid class as promising but still being characterised.[10][11][16] Registered studies are testing post-stroke depression and real-world postpartum outcomes.[7][9]
